In so many aspects of culture there are dichotomies where there shouldn't be. Even outside of politics: "there are two sides to every story" is a common saying, people strive to label characters as "good" and "evil," people dismiss others with "if you're not for us, you're against us," and "not hating" is the same as "supporting."

I'm familiar with the "divide and conquer" explanation, but that isn't enough. This isn't coming from external manipulators, people actually think this way. Why?

Why don't people recognize the spectrum of emotions and the strength of emotional response in favour of a binary good/bad?
Why is dichotomous thinking so pervasive?
It's like you said, with us or against us. It's tribal instinct.

The primary threat to hunter-gatherer societies was other groups of people. This lead to the evolution of a cognitive bias that makes humans categorize other humans into in-group and out-groups. Now, civilized life is a little more complex. Our health and safety are contingent upon cooperative relationships with people we've never met, and our own governments are often a greater threat to individuals than the citizens of other nations. But, the bias still persists because there hasn't been enough time or evolutionary pressure to remove it from our psyche.

One angle on this might be that dichotomizing might be part of effectively modelling complex systems. For one thing, a binary variable is the simplest non-trivial model there is. So from an efficiency standpoint it makes sense to start there, as well as from an Occam's razor standpoint of favoring parsimonious (simple) models. What may be more important (and I have no theoretical basis for this, but for all I know something like this may have been explored in learning theory) is that placing things into a Cartesian coordinate system allows the learning system to maintain a center/neutral point or behave stably even in extremely high-dimensional settings. I think humans are capable of more nuanced learning, but our core algorithm for motivation and behavior needs to be robust.

The conclusion would be that it's natural to accumulate many dichotomies over our lives, as there is more information to be modeled than we have time to sit and develop more nuanced models for (without sacrificing robustness)-- information is just flowing in rapidly and the basic/core algorithm is just throwing things onto dichotomies as the only way to integrate the information while remaining stable. Then (and I find this to be true personally) it would be that quietude or routine (reducing the inflow of information) and mindful reflection (engaging higher learning abilities) is necessary to start weeding out the dichotomies that don't make sense and building a more sophisticated model that also behaves stably.

Descartes.

"Cogito, ergo sum" and we've been more or less fucked ever since. Seriously. Once you reject Cartesian dualism, the world makes a whole lot more sense.

In everyday situations, I think most people recognize and understand various shades of gray, even when they just verbalize the dichotomous extremes. You would lose clarity in a conversation if you tried to go over every possibility within two extremes when talking with someone. Thus, I think dichotomous speech is more pervasive than dichotomous thought.

A strategy to alleviate dichotomous extremes in speech is to quickly mention the two extreme positions and then discuss a more realistic middle ground position in greater detail.

Binary "thinkers" don't have to prove that they're right about anything. All they have to do is find fault with the falsely dichotomous alternative. If they acknowledge a broader range of alternatives, then they're stuck having to justify their own preference, and that gets much more difficult.
